items.text: "Digital marketing" is not one skill with one finish line, it is a basket of very different skills with very different timelines.

blocks.heading: Questions to Set Your Own Realistic Timeline

items.text: Averages and course-marketing pages cannot tell you your own timeline.
SEO and analytics-heavy channels reward people who can wait months for a result without losing motivation.
How much runway do you actually have before you need income.

blocks.heading: Fast-Track Your Timeline with Real Campaign Experience

items.text: The single biggest lever for shortening the gap between "finished the course" and "job-ready" is not more course hours.
You do not need a client with a large budget to start.
Unpaid or low-stakes practice work is a legitimate and common way to build this kind of proof early, as long as you are honest about the scale of it when you describe it later.

blocks.heading: Timeline By Channel: Basics Vs Job-Ready
rows: SEO
A focused stretch of a few weeks to grasp keywords, on-page structure, and basic technical checks.
Roughly six months to a year of hands-on work on a real site before you can plan and defend a full strategy, because rankings themselves take months to move regardless of how fast you learn.
Search engines control the feedback loop, not you, you cannot practice your way to faster results.
Paid ads (Google, Meta)
A short test period to learn campaign structure, targeting, and the ad platform interface.
A few months of running real (even small) budgets across several campaigns before you can read data and adjust targeting without guessing.
Practicing with play money teaches the interface, not judgment, real budget pressure changes the decisions you make.
Social media marketing
Days to a couple of weeks to learn platform basics, content calendars, and posting cadence.
A few months of managing a real account with a real audience before you can defend a content strategy with actual engagement or conversion data.
Everyone thinks they already know this from personal use, which is exactly why the entry-level pool is the most crowded.
Content marketing / copywriting
A short stretch to learn structure, SEO-aware writing, and basic brief-following.
Several months to a year of writing for real briefs and real audiences before your writing reliably drives a measurable outcome, not just reads well.
Writing that sounds good and writing that converts are different skills, and only real audience feedback teaches the second one.
Email marketing and CRM
A focused couple of weeks to learn one platform (Mailchimp, HubSpot, or similar) and basic automation.
One to two months of building real sequences and reading open/click data before you can call yourself competent, the fastest channel to reach genuine competence.
The tool is easy; writing sequences that do not get ignored or unsubscribed from is the actual skill.

items.text: Whether you can open Google Ads Manager, GA4, or a CRM and produce a result without needing a tutorial mid-task.
A portfolio that states outcomes ("reduced cost per lead from X to Y") rather than only activities ("managed a Rs 50,000/month budget").
A live task or a short paid trial project, increasingly common in place of relying on certificates alone.
Genuine depth in at least one channel, plus familiarity with the standard tools for that channel, not shallow exposure to all five.
